questions.q: When FIIs suddenly sell large amounts of Indian stocks, what typically happens to the market and why?
options: The market rises because FIIs are exiting overvalued positions
The market falls because large selling pressure increases supply and reduces demand
The market stays flat because DIIs always buy what FIIs sell
The market rises because retail investors panic and buy cheap stocks
questions.explain: Large FII selling creates excess supply of shares, pushing prices down unless matched by equal buying demand.

questions.q: If the Nifty 50 index falls 10% but your stock falls 15%, what does this tell you about your stock?
options: Your stock is badly managed and should be sold immediately
Your stock is riskier (more volatile) than the overall market
Your stock is undervalued and will bounce back faster
Your stock has a higher dividend yield than index stocks
questions.explain: A stock falling more than the index indicates higher volatility and sensitivity to market movements—a measure of higher risk.

questions.q: Rahul invests ₹5,000 monthly via SIP when markets are high and low. After 2 years, markets fall 20%. Why is his average cost per unit lower than if he'd invested ₹60,000 on day one?
options: Because SIPs automatically buy only good stocks
Because his monthly investments buy more units when prices are lower, reducing his average cost
Because mutual fund managers charge less for SIP investors
Because the RBI guarantees minimum returns on SIP investments
questions.explain: SIPs buy more units when prices drop and fewer when prices rise, naturally lowering the average cost per unit over time.

questions.q: If the RBI raises interest rates from 6% to 7%, what happens to the price of existing bonds paying 5% fixed interest?
options: Bond prices rise because interest rates and bond prices move together
Bond prices fall because new bonds now offer better returns, making old bonds less attractive
Bond prices stay the same because the coupon is locked in
Bond prices rise because investors flee to safer investments
questions.explain: When new bonds offer higher rates, existing lower-rate bonds become less valuable, so their prices drop to remain competitive.

questions.q: You bought a stock for ₹100 and sold it for ₹150 after 2 years. On this ₹50 gain, which tax applies under Indian law?
options: Long-term capital gains tax of 10% (or 20% with indexation)
Short-term capital gains tax of 15%
Income tax as per your slab rate (30-40%)
GST of 18% on the profit amount
questions.explain: Holding over 12 months qualifies as long-term; LTCG is taxed at 10% without indexation or 20% with indexation benefit under Indian tax law.
